name: RMM

paper.title: In Prospect and Retrospect: Reflective Memory Management for Long-term Personalized Dialogue Agents

construction.unit: memory entry: (topic summary, raw dialogue turns it came from)
construction.kept_as: LLM topic summary as search key + verbatim turns
construction.processing: at session end an LLM splits the session into topics, writing one personal summary per topic with its turn ids, for each speaker
construction.writer: prompted LLM (model not named for this step; the generator is Gemini-1.5-Flash)

organization.structure: flat memory bank of topic entries
organization.index: dense embeddings of topic summaries (Contriever default; Stella, GTE tested)

management.operations: each new topic memory is compared with its Top-K most similar entries; LLM chooses Add() or Merge(index, merged_summary)
management.conflicts: handled by merge: the LLM rewrites the old summary with the new information

retrieval.candidates: dense retriever Top-K=20 over topic summaries
retrieval.selection: learned reranker (residual linear adapters on query and memory embeddings, dot product) with Gumbel-softmax sampling keeps Top-M=5; reranker trained online by REINFORCE from the LLM's citations
retrieval.budget: Top-M = 5 entries (10 with Top-K = 50 in Table 5)

use.context: the 5 memories, each as personal summary plus its original turns, with the current session
use.reasoning: one LLM call writes the response and cites the memories it used

classify.note: The reranker is a small learned model on embeddings, not a cross-encoder; it is updated online by REINFORCE from the answer LLM's citations.

stages.ingestion: Memory is written once per finished session; the session's turns are passed whole to the extraction prompt.
stages.construction: Prospective Reflection: an LLM decomposes the session into topics and writes a concise personal summary for each, with references to the turn ids it came from; this is done separately for each speaker.
stages.organization: A flat memory bank of (topic summary, raw dialogue) entries; the summary is the retrieval key.
stages.update: Each new topic memory is compared with the Top-K most similar existing entries, and an LLM either adds it or merges it into one of them with a rewritten summary.
stages.retrieval: A frozen dense retriever returns Top-K=20 entries; a lightweight reranker (residual linear maps on query and memory embeddings, dot-product scores) samples Top-M=5 with the Gumbel trick at τ = 0.5.
stages.answer: The LLM sees the current session and the 5 memories (summary plus original turns), writes the reply and cites the memories it used in the same call.
stages.learning: Retrospective Reflection: each retrieved memory gets +1 if cited and −1 if not, and REINFORCE (baseline 0.5, lr 1e-3, batch 4) updates only the reranker, online during the conversation.

summary: Topic-level memories (LLM summary as key, original turns as content) are written and merged at session end, and a small reranker over retriever embeddings is trained online with REINFORCE using the answer LLM's own citations as reward.
notes: arXiv v2 (2025-07-28) read from the PDF; arXiv comment and ACL Anthology (2025.acl-long.413, pp. 8416-8439) give ACL 2025 main. No official code was found (paper gives no link; only an unofficial third-party plugin exists on GitHub). Baselines MemoryBank and LD-Agent were re-implemented with the LongMemEval codebase (App. A.4). The LLM for memory extraction/merge is not named; Gemini-1.5-Flash is the generator. LongMemEval variant (S/M/oracle) is not stated.

sources.code_note: No official code: the paper and the ACL Anthology page link none, and a GitHub search found only an unofficial re-implementation, which is not used here. Everything follows the paper, Algorithm 1, Figures 2-3 and the prompts in App. D.

headline: A memory entry pairs an LLM topic summary (the search key) with the original turns, and the answer model reads both.
The only learned part is a small reranker on top of a frozen retriever; its reward is whether the answer LLM cited each memory (+1) or not (−1).
The reranker is updated after every response, so it learns during the conversation itself; the paper does not separate this from the evaluation questions.

units.name: Memory entry
units.role: one topic from one or more turns of a past session
units.made_by: LLM extraction at session end, then LLM Add/Merge against similar entries

fields.name: topic summary
fields.what: concise personal summary of one speaker's experiences, preferences or background for one topic; rewritten on merge

fields.name: raw dialogue
fields.what: the original turns the summary references (turn ids)

fields.name: embedding
fields.what: retriever embedding of the entry, adapted by the reranker's W_m

units.name: Reranker
units.role: learned scoring layer between retriever and LLM

fields.name: W_q, W_m
fields.what: linear maps added residually to query and memory embeddings (q′ = q + W_q q, m′ = m + W_m m)

write.how: at session end an LLM returns JSON {summary, reference: [turn ids]} per topic, run once for each speaker; NO_TRAIT if nothing personal
retrieve the Top-K most similar existing entries for each new topic memory
LLM outputs Add() or Merge(index, merged_summary), possibly several actions

read.scores: dot product of adapted embeddings q′·m′ plus Gumbel noise, softmax at τ
read.how: sample Top-M from the perturbed distribution
one LLM call writes the response and lists the indices of useful memories, or [NO_CITE]
reward +1 for cited, −1 for not cited; REINFORCE Δφ = η(R − b)∇ log P(M_M | q, M_K)

answer_context.sees: 5 memories, each a personal summary followed by its original turns, plus the current session
answer_context.format: "Memory [i]: summary" followed by its turns, with instructions to cite indices [i] (App. D.2)
includes: raw turns referenced by each summary

compression.basis: Not reported: the paper gives no token counts for memory or context.

open_questions: Is the reranker trained on the same questions it is scored on? Algorithm 1 updates it after every response, and the paper describes no separate training stream except for the offline pretraining study in §8.6.
How is Recall@5 computed when retrieved items are merged topic entries rather than the annotated turns?
Which LongMemEval split (S, M or oracle) is used is not stated, so the numbers cannot be placed next to other papers' LongMemEval results.

glance.a: A topic: an LLM-written personal summary (the search key) plus the original turns it refers to.
Once per session, when it ends; new topics are added or merged into similar old ones by an LLM.
Yes: a small learned reranker on the retriever's embeddings keeps 5 of 20 by Gumbel sampling.

glance.q: What is learned, and from what?
glance.a: Only the reranker, by REINFORCE: +1 when the answer LLM cites a memory, −1 when it does not.

glance.q: What does the answer model read?
glance.a: The current session and 5 memories, each with its summary and original turns.

text: When a session ends, an LLM splits it into topics and writes one personal summary per topic with the turn ids it came from, for each speaker.
Each new topic is checked against the most similar entries in the bank, and the LLM either adds it or merges it into one of them.

key_numbers.label: Memory written
key_numbers.value: once per session, at its end

components.model: prompted LLM (model not named for this step)
learned residual linear adapters + dot product on the retriever embeddings (not a cross-encoder)

discussion.takeaway: Organise memory by topic rather than by turn or session, and let the answer model's own citations train a small reranker online. On LongMemEval with GTE this lifts accuracy from 63.6 (turn-level RAG) to 70.4.

claims.claim: RMM beats all baselines on MSC and LongMemEval.
claims.evidence: GTE: MSC METEOR 33.4 vs 27.5, BERT 57.1 vs 52.1; LongMemEval Recall@5 69.8 vs 62.4, Acc 70.4 vs 63.6 over RAG. Table 1, §8.1

claims.claim: Both reflections help, and the reranker is needed for the RL signal.
claims.evidence: Contriever: RAG 58.8 → +PR 59.6, +RR 60.2, both 61.2 Acc; fine-tuning the retriever instead drops to 31.0. Table 2, §8.2
Overall precision 87.6, recall 85.8, F1 86.7 against a Gemini-1.5-Pro judge. Table 3, §8.3

claims.claim: Topic granularity approaches the best per-instance fixed granularity.
claims.evidence: On 100 LongMemEval samples (GTE): Recall@5 78 (PR) vs 47 turn, 69 session, 86 best; Acc 49 vs 29, 34, 58. Fig. 4, §8.5

claims.claim: More retrieved and kept memories help.

limits: RL reranking can be computationally expensive for large-scale or real-time use.
Text-only; multimodal dialogue is not handled.
The memory update mechanism may need further work for dynamically evolving long-term interactions.
reading: The reranker is updated after every response (Algorithm 1), and no separate training stream is described for the main tables, so the reported scores include learning on the evaluation conversations themselves.
The gain from the full system over plain RAG with Contriever is small on LongMemEval accuracy (58.8 → 61.2) and larger on MSC METEOR (24.8 → 30.8); the headline 70.4 needs the GTE-7B retriever.
MemoryBank and LD-Agent are listed with 'specific' retrievers in Table 1, but App. A.4 says they were re-implemented in the LongMemEval codebase with Contriever as default retriever.
The answer model reads the original turns as well as the summaries, so the Prospective Reflection gain mixes a better search key with different context boundaries; no run separates the two.
The granularity study (Fig. 4) uses 100 samples and reports PR at 49 accuracy, well below the 70.4 of Table 1 with the same retriever and generator; the paper does not explain the gap.
No token, latency or LLM-call costs are reported, although extraction and merging add LLM calls at every session end.

abstract.text: RMM is a memory design for personalized dialogue agents that addresses two problems: memory cut at fixed turn or session boundaries, and retrievers that never adapt. Looking forward, it summarises each finished session into topic-level memories (a summary plus the turns it came from) and merges them with related existing ones. Looking back, it trains a small reranker on top of a frozen retriever with online reinforcement learning, rewarding memories the answer model cites. With Gemini-1.5-Flash it beats RAG, MemoryBank and LD-Agent baselines on MSC and LongMemEval, reaching 70.4% LongMemEval accuracy with the GTE retriever.
